rv.q: I came out rattled as I have rarely been rattled by any theater experience, devastated and blissful at the same improbable time.
It's a journey that leads not just to a healthy end — this hip earth mother recovers — but an uplifting one.
Ensler does not falter, sparing none of the gritty, gruesome details, even as she tries to inject some humor into her own personal horror story.
Rather than using Ms. Ensler's illness to illuminate the world's, it too often borrows from the world's suffering in an effort to legitimize her own.
It's simultaneously appalling—surely she can hear the narcissism?—and true.
It's hard to avoid the feeling that In the Body of the World would have been more effective as a simple lecture, shorn of the affectations...
This intellectually ambitious, uneven but fascinating, often anti-theatrical piece of theater by adapting the memoir Retour à Reims by the French philosopher Didier Eribon.
Above all, there is an unmistakable air of honesty throughout the 80-minutes proceedings that keeps us listening.
What makes “In The Body of the World” especially worthwhile is the production.

Plan on staying in the theatre for five or ten minutes after the play is done, as designers Myung Hee Cho (set and costume), Jen Schriever (lights), Finn Ross (projections) and M.L. Dogg and Sam Lerner (sound) provide a perfect atmosphere for contemplating our better nature.
The author-performer quickly balances self-deprecating humor and cutting observations with her social commentary.
The story that Ensler tells over 80 minutes is smart, harrowing, surprisingly humorous, and can serve as an inspiration for anyone, female and otherwise, confronted by serious illness.

“Ensler keeps the play afloat with her frankness and humor, even when she unabashedly displays her wounds and describes parts of her body removed or mangled. We accompany her to New York City where she first tries Memorial Sloan Kettering, but settles on Beth Israel, where her doctor treats her like a real, living, breathing person.
Diane Paulus's direction is a huge plus, tying together the disparate elements with clarity and sensitivity.

"Ensler doesn't tiptoe around a topic. She doesn't mince words. That unblinking, even brutal, bluntness is a strength in her solo play...Humor is another plus...She's not shy about revealing her scars - physical and psychic.
She has an uplifting and often riveting tale to tell, and, aided by Diane Paulus's focused direction, she tells it sharply and movingly.
She's a warm, charming, grounded narrator...Like a mirror image of her own life, the story is choppy and off-roads more often than it stays any particular course.
She is smart, funny, mostly fearless, empathetic — an engaging if sometimes tangent-plagued raconteur.
And yet I can't escape the nagging feeling that Ensler, with all the goodwill in the world, has created a piece that is profoundly unhelpful.
And what a wondrous storm it is!
Ensler's frank vulnerability and synthesis of the personal and political reaches thrilling new heights in director Diane Paulus' striking production for Manhattan Theatre Club.
"In the Body of the World" is a critical piece of art.
A frank, fierce, and surprisingly funny look at the impact of Ensler's uterine cancer diagnosis, juxtaposing the limits of medical science with the healing power of feminist political engagement.
So compelling is this cancer-Congo-nature triangle, the show sinks a little whenever Ensler steps outside of it.
Ensler is a likable, sharp-talking guide through her excruciating tour through hell.

If you are drawn in, you’ll be held tight, but if not, you’ll walk out, like I did, bypassing the invitation, feeling that you did truly experience something powerful, but just not the internalized connection you might have been hoping for.
I'm sorry that Ensler had to go through such a harrowing experience but I'm also sorry that her show dragged me through it.

But Eve Ensler’s daring, delightful one-woman show, In the Body of the World, which opened tonight at Manhattan Theatre Club’s Stage I at City Center, is bursting with the affirmation of life and the celebration of joy.

In the Body also requires the presence of this daring artist’s own body—from her shaved head (don’t let that silken Louise Brooks helmet fool you) to both her surgical and psychological scars—to make its searingly poignant and satirically comic points.

cn.t: Critics largely praise Ensler's raw, fearless performance connecting her cancer battle to global women's issues, though some find the show's scope overly ambitious and self-involved. Her humor and vulnerability resonate powerfully.
